passages.original: In mea enim patria rusticitatis uernacula deus uenter est et de die uiuitur: sanctior est ille, qui ditior est. accessit huic patellae iuxta tritum populi sermone prouerbium dignum operculum, Lupicinus sacerdos — secundum illud quoque, de quo semel in uita Crassum ait risisse Lucilius: \'similem habent labra lactucam asino cardus comedente\' —, uidelicet ut perforatam nauem debilis gubernator regat et caecus caecos ducat in foueam talisque sit rector, quales illi qui reguntur.
passages.english: For in my homeland, where boorishness is native, the belly is god and people live for the day: the holier man is the one who is richer. To this dish, according to the proverb worn smooth in popular speech, a fitting lid has been added, the priest Lupicinus. This fits that saying too, at which, Lucilius says, Crassus laughed once in his life: 'the lips have lettuce to match when a donkey eats thistles'. So a feeble helmsman steers a holed ship, the blind lead the blind into the pit, and the ruler is like those who are ruled.
passages.notes: 'Lucilius' as transmitted; the anecdote of Crassus laughing once in his life is attributed to Lucilius.

passages.original: nec falsam dedit, quamquam in re non uera, sententiam. quid enim est, ut ita dicam, tam praesens inter absentes, quam per epistulas et adloqui et audire quos diligas? nam et rudes illi Italiae homines, quos cascos Ennius appellat, qui sibi, ut in Rhetoricis Cicero ait, uictu fero uitam requirebant, ante chartae et membranarum usum aut in dedolatis ex ligno codicellis aut in corticibus arborum mutua epistularum adloquia missitabant; unde et portitores earum tabellarios et scriptores a libris arborum librarios uocauere.
passages.english: Nor did he give a false sentiment, although on a matter that was not true. For what is there, so to speak, so present among the absent as to address and to hear by letters those whom you love? For even those rude men of Italy, whom Ennius calls *casci* [ancients], who, as Cicero says in the Rhetorica, sought their living by wild food, before the use of paper and parchment used to send one another the conversations of letters either on little tablets hewn from wood or on the bark of trees. Hence they called the carriers of these *tabellarii* [tablet-men], and the writers *librarii*, from the *libri* [inner bark] of trees.

passages.original: Doctissimi quique Graecorum, de quibus pro Flacco agens luculente Tullius ait: ingenita leuitas et erudita uanitas, regum suorum uel principum laudes accepta mercede dicebant. hoc ego nunc faciens pretium posco pro laudibus.
passages.english: All the most learned of the Greeks, of whom Tullius, pleading for Flaccus, splendidly says, "inborn levity and learned vanity," used to pronounce the praises of their kings or princes after receiving a fee. Doing this now, I ask a price for my praises.
passages.notes: Tullius is Cicero (Pro Flacco).

passages.original: nonnulli uero in superioribus consentientes in extrema parte dissentiunt. nam superliminare sublatum illo tempore praedicant, quando uelum templi scissum est et uniuersa domus Israhel erroris nube confusa, quando Iosephus refert sacerdotes ex adytis templi uirtutum caelestium audisse uocem: \'transeamus ex his sedibus\'.
passages.english: Some, however, who agree in the earlier points, disagree in the last part. For they declare that the lintel was removed at that time when the veil of the temple was torn and the whole house of Israel was confounded by a cloud of error, when Josephus relates that the priests heard from the inner sanctuary of the temple the voice of the heavenly powers: 'Let us depart from these seats.'

passages.original: Multi super hoc sermone diuersa finxerunt, e quibus noster Hilarius in commentariis Mathei ita posuit: \'osanna\' Hebraico sermone significatur\'redemptiodomusDauid\'. primum \'redemptio\' lingua Hebraea \'pheduth> interpretatur, deinde \'domus\' \'beth\', \'dauid\' uero in hoc loco non esse nomen insertum omnibus patet.
passages.english: Many have invented various things about this word, among whom our Hilary, in his commentaries on Matthew, put it thus: 'hosanna' in the Hebrew language means 'redemption of the house of David.' First, 'redemption' in the Hebrew language is rendered 'pheduth', then 'house' is 'beth', and it is plain to all that 'David' is not a name inserted in this place.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'redemptiodomusDauid' read as 'redemptio domus Dauid'; 'pheduth>' as 'pheduth'.

passages.original: at, si tibi placet scire, quot molestiis uirgo libera, quot uxor adstricta sit, lege Tertulliani ad amicum philosophum et de uirginitate alios libellos et beati Cypriani uolumen egregium et papae Damasi super hac re uersu prosaque conposita et Ambrosii nostri quae nuper ad sororem scripsit opuscula. in quibus tanto se fudit eloquio, ut, quidquid ad laudem uirginum pertinet, exquisierit, ordinarit, expresserit.
passages.english: But if you wish to know how many troubles a virgin is free of and how many a wife is bound by, read Tertullian's [book] To a Philosopher Friend and his other little books on virginity, and the excellent volume of the blessed Cyprian, and what Pope Damasus composed on this subject in verse and prose, and the short works which our Ambrose recently wrote to his sister. In these he poured himself out with such eloquence that he has searched out, set in order and expressed whatever pertains to the praise of virgins.

passages.original: Ad quod nos, quia dictandi angustia coartamur, breuiter respondemus siue septuaginta interpretes siue apostolos id curasse, ut, quoniam prima ecclesia ex ludaeis fuerat congregata, nihil ob credentium scandalum innouarent, sed ita, ut a paruo inbiberant, traderent, postea uero quam in uniuersas gentes euangelii dilatatus est sermo, non potuisse semel suscepta mutari, licet et illud in libris suis, quos iSrjnTjttxoot uocat, Origenes adserat, propter uernaculum linguae uniuscuiusque idioma non posse ita apud alios sonare, ut apud suos dicta sunt, et multo esse melius ininterpretata ponere, quam uim interpretatione tenuare.
passages.english: To this, since we are constrained by the pressure of dictating, we reply briefly that either the Seventy translators or the apostles took care that, since the first church had been gathered from the Jews, they should introduce nothing new, on account of offence to believers, but should hand on [things] as they had imbibed them from childhood; and that afterwards, when the word of the gospel had spread to all nations, what had once been received could not be changed. Origen too asserts in his books which he calls *Exegetika* (Exegetical Books) that, because of the native idiom of each language, [words] cannot sound among others as they were spoken among their own people, and that it is much better to set them down untranslated than to weaken their force by translation.
passages.notes: The Greek title is garbled in the scan ('iSrjnTjttxoot'); read as Exegetika. 'ludaeis' read as 'Iudaeis'.

passages.original: quamuis enim dicere audeant: ego ciuitas firma, ciuitas, quae obpugnatur, -nullus hostili exercitu obsidente securus est. nemo, ut beatus Cyprianus ait, satis tutus periculo proximus. exemplar epistulae, si accipere uoluerit (ptXoitov(oto\'tt] nostra Marcella, tribuito et memento mei obsecrans, ut dominus Iesus conterat satanan sub pedibus nostris uelociter.
passages.english: For although they may dare to say, "I am a strong city, a city that is besieged," no one is secure while an enemy army is besieging. No one, as the blessed Cyprian says, is safe enough when close to danger. Give a copy of the letter, if she wishes to receive it, to our Marcella, lover of toil, and remember me, praying that the Lord Jesus may swiftly crush Satan under our feet.
passages.notes: The Greek epithet for Marcella is garbled in the scan; probably φιλοπονωτάτη ('most hard-working').

passages.original: Scripsit igitur Varro XLV libros Antiquitatum, IIII De uita populi Romani, Imaginum XV, Aofiatoptxwv LXXVI, De lingua Latina XXV, Disciplinarum VIIII, De sermone Latino V, Quaestionum Plautinarum V, Annalium III, De origine linguae Latinae III, De poematis III, De originibus scaenicis III, De scaenicis actionibus III, De actis scaenicis III, De descriptionibus III, De proprietate scriptorum III, De bibliothecis III, De lectionibus III, De similitudine uerborum III, Legationum III, Suasionum III, De Pompeio III, Singulares X, De personis III, De iure ciuili XV, \'Emofirjv Antiquitatum ex libris XLII libros VIIII, Επιτομὴν ex Imaginum libris XV libros IIII, Επιτομὴν de lingua Latina ex libris XV libros VIIII, De principiis numerorum libros VIIII, Rerum rusticarum libros III, De ualetudine tuenda librum I, De sua uita libros III, De forma philosophiae libros III, Rerum urbanarum libros III, Sa.tirarum Menippearum libros CL, Poematum libros X, Orationum libros XXII, Pseudotragoediarum libros VI, Satirarum libros IIII et alia plurima, quae enumerare longum est.
passages.english: Varro, then, wrote 45 books of Antiquities; 4 On the Life of the Roman People; 15 of Portraits; 76 of Logistorici; 25 On the Latin Language; 9 of Disciplines; 5 On Latin Speech; 5 of Plautine Questions; 3 of Annals; 3 On the Origin of the Latin Language; 3 On Poems; 3 On Theatrical Origins; 3 On Theatrical Performances; 3 On Theatrical Records; 3 On Descriptions; 3 On the Distinctive Features of Writers; 3 On Libraries; 3 On Readings; 3 On the Similarity of Words; 3 of Embassies; 3 of Persuasions; 3 On Pompey; 10 Single books; 3 On Persons; 15 On Civil Law; an Epitome of the Antiquities from 42 books, in 9 books; an Epitome from the 15 books of Portraits, in 4 books; an Epitome On the Latin Language from 15 books, in 9 books; On the Principles of Numbers, 9 books; On Country Matters, 3 books; On Preserving Health, 1 book; On His Own Life, 3 books; On the Form of Philosophy, 3 books; On City Matters, 3 books; Menippean Satires, 150 books; Poems, 10 books; Speeches, 22 books; Pseudo-tragedies, 6 books; Satires, 4 books; and very many others which it would take long to enumerate.
passages.notes: Scanning errors: 'Aofiatoptxwv' read as Logistoricōn (Logistorici); ''Emofirjv' read as Epitomēn.

passages.original: nisi quod non eius culpae adscribendum est, qui Hebraei sermonis ignarus fuit, Graecarum quoque litterarum quandam aurulam ceperat, sed Heliodori presbyteri, quo ille familiariter usus ea, quae intellegere non poterat, quomodo ab Origene essent dicta, quaerebat. qui, quia in hoc psalmo commentarium Origenis inuenire non potuit, opinionem magis insinuare suam quam inscientiam uoluit confiteri, quam ille sumptam claro sermone disseruit et alienum errorem disertius exsecutus est.
passages.english: Except that this is not to be ascribed to the fault of him who was ignorant of the Hebrew language and had caught only a certain faint breath of Greek letters too, but to the priest Heliodorus, whom he consulted as a close friend, asking how things he could not understand had been said by Origen. He, because he could not find Origen's commentary on this psalm, preferred to slip in his own opinion rather than confess his ignorance; and [the other], taking this up, set it out in clear language and expounded another man's error more eloquently.
passages.notes: 'aurulam' (a faint breeze, i.e. a slight acquaintance) is a rare diminutive.

passages.original: Ambrosius, quo chartas, sumptus, notarios ministrante tam innumerabiles libros uere Adamantius et noster XaXvivtspo; explicauit, in quadam epistula, quam ad eundem de Athenis scripserat, refert numquam se cibos Origene praesente sine lectione sumpsisse, numquam uenisse somnum, nisi e fratribus aliquis sacris litteris personaret, hoc diebus egisse uel noctibus, ut et lectio orationem susciperet et oratio lectionem.
passages.english: Ambrose, who supplied the paper, expenses and stenographers by which our truly 'Adamantius' and 'Chalcenterus' produced so countless a number of books, relates in a certain letter which he had written to him from Athens that he never took food in Origen's presence without reading, that sleep never came unless one of the brothers was sounding forth the sacred writings, and that he did this by day and by night, so that reading followed upon prayer and prayer upon reading.
passages.notes: Greek garbled in the scan ('XaXvivtspo;'); read as Χαλκέντερος ('brazen-guts', i.e. indefatigable).

passages.original: Origenes, Methodius, Eusebius, Apollinaris multis uersuum milibus scribunt aduersus Celsum et Porphyrium: considerate, quibus argumentis et quam lubricis problemata diaboli spiritu contexta subuertant et, quia interdum coguntur loqui, non quod sentiunt, sed quod necesse est, dicantur esse gentiles.
passages.english: Origen, Methodius, Eusebius and Apollinaris write against Celsus and Porphyry in many thousands of lines: consider with what arguments and how slippery ones they overturn the problems woven by the spirit of the devil, and how, because they are sometimes compelled to say not what they think but what is necessary, they are said to be pagans.
passages.notes: The final clause is awkwardly transmitted; it appears to mean they say what is needed against the pagans. Reading uncertain.

passages.original: scio Romae hanc esse consuetudinem, ut fideles semper Christi corpus accipiant, quod nec reprehendo nec probo — unusquisque enim in sensu suo abundat —, sed ipsorum conscientiam conuenio, qui eodem die post coitum communicant et iuxta Persium noctem flumine purgant, quare ad martyres ire non audeant, quare non ingrediantur ecclesias. an alius in publico, alius domi Christus est? quod in ecclesia non licet, nec domi licet. nihil deo clausum est et tenebrae quoque lucent apud eum.
passages.english: I know that at Rome there is this custom, that the faithful always receive the body of Christ, which I neither blame nor approve — for let each abound in his own sense — but I appeal to the conscience of those who communicate on the same day after intercourse and, as Persius has it, purge the night in the river: why do they not dare to go to the martyrs, why do they not enter the churches? Is there one Christ in public and another at home? What is not lawful in church is not lawful at home either. Nothing is closed to God, and even darkness shines before him.

passages.original: Simpliciter loquar: nos, secundum quod scriptum est, nec oculo nostro parcimus, ut non effodiamus eum, si nosscandalizauerit, nec manui nec pedi, si nobis scandalum fecerint. et uos ergo, siue oculi nostri siue mamis siue pes fueritis, similia sustinebitis. quis enim catholicorum possit aequo animo sustinere et eorum, qui fidem suam bonis operibus exornant, ut audiant Origenis doctrinam atque consilium et credant praeclarae illius praedicationi: (non potest filius uidere patrem neque spiritus sanctus uidere filiiim\'?
passages.english: I will speak plainly: we, according to what is written, do not spare even our own eye, but pluck it out, if it has caused us to stumble, nor our hand nor our foot, if they have made us stumble. You too, then, whether you are our eye or hand or foot, will undergo the like. For which of the catholics, and of those who adorn their faith with good works, could bear with equanimity to hear the teaching and counsel of Origen and to believe that famous preaching of his: "The Son cannot see the Father, nor can the Holy Spirit see the Son"?
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'nosscandalizauerit' = 'nos scandalizauerit', 'mamis' = 'manus', 'filiiim' = 'filium'. The construction 'et eorum, qui...' is awkward; rendered as 'and of those who'.

passages.original: haec in libris rcsplap/wv scribuntur, his uerbis legimus et ita locutus est Origenes: sicut enim incongruum est dicere, quod possit filius uidere patrem, sic inconsequens est opinari, quod spiritus sanctus possit uidere filium.
passages.english: These things are written in the books Peri Archōn (On First Principles); we read them in these words, and thus Origen spoke: "For just as it is incongruous to say that the Son can see the Father, so it is inconsistent to suppose that the Holy Spirit can see the Son."
passages.notes: 'rcsplap/wv' is a garbled scan of the Greek title Περὶ ἀρχῶν (On First Principles).

passages.original: illud quoque quis Origene dicente patiatur, quod animae angeli fuerint in caelis et, postquam peccauerint in supernis, deiectas esse in istum mundum et quasi in tumulos et sepulchra sic in corpora ista relegatas poenas antiquorum luere peccatorum et corpora credentium non templa Christi esse, sed carceres damnatorum?
passages.english: Who, too, could tolerate Origen when he says that souls were angels in the heavens, and that after they sinned on high they were cast down into this world, and, banished into these bodies as into tombs and sepulchres, pay the penalties of their ancient sins; and that the bodies of believers are not temples of Christ but prisons of the condemned?

passages.original: ubi apostolica doctrina, quae in ecclesiis Christi hucusque perdurat? ubi illa benedictio ad Adam et ad semen eius et ad Noe et ad filios eius: crescite et multiplicamini et replete terram? iam enim non erit benedictio, sed maledictio iuxta Origenem, qui angelos uertit in animas et de sublimi fastigio dignitatis facit ad inferiora doscendere, quasi deus generi humano non possit animas per nedictionem dare, nisi angeli peccauerint, et tot in caelis ruinae sint, quot in terra natiuitates.
passages.english: Where is the apostolic teaching, which has endured in the churches of Christ up to now? Where is that blessing to Adam and his seed, and to Noah and his sons: "Increase and multiply and fill the earth"? For now it will be not a blessing but a curse, according to Origen, who turns angels into souls and makes them descend from the lofty summit of dignity to lower things, as though God could not give souls to the human race through a blessing unless angels had sinned, and there were as many falls in heaven as there are births on earth.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'doscendere' = 'descendere', 'per nedictionem' = 'per benedictionem'.

passages.original: dimittenda nobis est doctrina apostolorum et prophetarum et legis et ipsius domini saluatoris in euangelio pertonantis: e contrario Origenes praecipit et legem dat — ut non dicam: constringit discipulos suos —, ne quis oret in caelum: ascendere, ne peius iterum peccans, quam in terris ante peccauerat, praecipitetur in mundum.
passages.english: [On this view] we must abandon the teaching of the apostles and prophets and of the law, and of the Lord Saviour himself thundering in the gospel: Origen, on the contrary, instructs and lays down a law — not to say binds his disciples — that no one should pray to ascend into heaven, lest, sinning again worse than he had sinned before on earth, he be hurled down into the world.

passages.original: quis autem patienter ferat Origenem lubricis argumentationibus resurrectionem carnis huius negantem, sicut declarat manifestissime in uolumiue Explanationum primi psalmi et in aliis multis locis? aut quis audiat in tertio caelo donantem nobis Origenem paradisum et illum, quem scriptura commemorat, de terra ad caelestia transferentem et omnes arbores, quae scribuntur in Genesi, allegorice intellegentem, scilicet quod arbores angelicae fortitudines sint, cum hoc ueritas non recipiat?
passages.english: And who would patiently bear Origen denying, with slippery arguments, the resurrection of this flesh, as he declares most plainly in the volume of his Explanations of the First Psalm and in many other places? Or who would listen to Origen granting us paradise in the third heaven, and transferring the one that Scripture records from earth to the heavenly realms, and understanding all the trees written of in Genesis allegorically — namely, that the trees are angelic powers — when the truth does not admit this?
passages.notes: 'uolumiue' corrected to 'uolumine'.

passages.original: si autem aqua, quae cernitur, uere aqua est, necesse est, ut et ficus uera sit et alia ligna et Adam uerus statim a principio plasmatus in corpore sicut Eua et non in phantasmate et post ruinam, ut uult Origenes, propter peccatum postea corpus acceperit.
passages.english: But if the water that is seen is truly water, it necessarily follows that the fig tree too is real, and the other trees, and that Adam was real, formed in a body right from the beginning, as was Eve, and not in a phantom, and [did not], as Origen would have it, receive a body only later, after the fall, because of sin.
passages.notes: The sense requires a negation carried over to the final clause; supplied in brackets.

passages.original: bene dicis: quando ponit (tertium caelum\' et postea addidit \'et in paradisum\', ostendit alibi esse caelum et alibi paradisum. illas uero praestigias quis non statim abiciat atque contemnat dicente Origene de aquis, quae super firmamentum sunt, non esse aquas, sed fortitudines quasdam angelicae. potestatis, et rursum aquas, quae super terram sunt, hoc est sub firmamento, esse uirtutes contrarias, id est daemones?
passages.english: You say well: when he puts "the third heaven" and afterwards adds "and into paradise", he shows that heaven is in one place and paradise in another. But who would not at once reject and despise those conjuring tricks, when Origen says of the waters that are above the firmament that they are not waters but certain powers of angelic might, and again that the waters that are above the earth, that is, under the firmament, are opposing powers, that is, demons?
passages.notes: 'angelicae. potestatis' has a stray full stop, ignored.

passages.original: decet enim honestatem tuam hanc magis habere sollicitudinem et uti scrupulositate, quae digna est ecclesiae Christi et populis, qui tibi crediti sunt. Palladium uero Galatam, qui quondam carus nobis fuit et nunc misericordia dei indiget, caue, quia Origenis heresem praedicat et docet, ne forte aliquos de populo tibi credito ad peruersitatem sui inducat erroris.
passages.english: For it befits your honour rather to have this concern, and to exercise a scrupulousness worthy of the church of Christ and of the peoples entrusted to you. As for Palladius the Galatian, who was once dear to us and now stands in need of God's mercy, beware of him, for he preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen, lest he perhaps lead some of the people entrusted to you into the perversity of his own error.

passages.original: unde et sapiens ille Graeciae, cum expletis centum et septem annis se mori cerneret, dixisse fertur dolere, quod tunc egrederetur e uita, quando sapere coepisset; Plato octogesimo et uno anno scribens est mortuus; Isocrates nonaginta et nouem annos in docendi scribendique labore conpleuit; taceo ceteros philosophos, Pythagoram, Democritum, Xenocratem, Zenonem, Cleanthem, qui iam aetate longaeua in sapientiae studiis floruerunt: ad poetas uenio, Homerum, Hesiodum, Simonidem, Stesichorum, qui grandes natu cygneum nescio quid et solito dulcius uicina morte cecinerunt.
passages.english: Hence also that wise man of Greece, when, having completed one hundred and seven years, he saw that he was dying, is reported to have said that he grieved that he was leaving life just when he had begun to be wise; Plato died at eighty-one while writing; Isocrates completed ninety-nine years in the labour of teaching and writing; I say nothing of the other philosophers, Pythagoras, Democritus, Xenocrates, Zeno, Cleanthes, who flourished in the pursuit of wisdom when already of great age: I come to the poets, Homer, Hesiod, Simonides, Stesichorus, who, advanced in years, sang with death near something swan-like and sweeter than usual.
passages.notes: The 'wise man of Greece' is unnamed here; traditionally Theophrastus.

passages.original: recitauit iudicibus: et tantum sapientiae in aetate iam fracta specimen dedit, ut seueritatem tribunalium in theatri fauorem uerteret. nec mirum, cum etiam Cato, Romani generis disertissimus, censorius iam et senex, Graecas litteras nec erubuerit nec desperauerit discere. certe Homerus refert, quod de lingua Nestoris iam uetuli et paene decrepiti dulcior melle oratio fluxerit.
passages.english: he read [it] to the judges, and gave such a proof of wisdom at an age already broken that he turned the severity of the court into the applause of a theatre. Nor is it surprising, since even Cato, the most eloquent of the Roman race, when already an ex-censor and an old man, was neither ashamed nor despaired of learning Greek letters. Certainly Homer relates that from the tongue of Nestor, when already aged and almost decrepit, there flowed speech sweeter than honey.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the context shows the subject is Sophocles, who read his recently written Oedipus to the judges when accused of senility by his sons.

passages.original: illud\', aiebat, \'Tertulliani, istud Cypriani, hoc Lactantii, illud Hilarii est. sic Minucius Felix, ita Uictorinus, in hunc modum est locutus Arnobius\'. me quoque, quia pro sodalitate auunculi diligebat, interdum proferebat in medium. lectione quoque adsidua et meditatione diuturna pectus suum bibliothecam fecerat Christi.
passages.english: "That," he used to say, "is Tertullian's, this Cyprian's, this Lactantius', that Hilary's. Thus Minucius Felix [spoke], so Victorinus, in this manner Arnobius spoke." Me too, because he loved me for his friendship with my uncle, he would sometimes bring forward [as an example]. By constant reading and long meditation he had made his breast a library of Christ.

passages.original: Naeuius poeta: pati, inquit, necesse est multa mortalem mala. unde et Niobam, quia multum fleuerit, in lapidem et in diuersas bestias (conuersas alias ut Hecubam in canem) commutatam finxit antiquitas, et Hesiodus natales hominum plangens gaudet in funere, prudenterque Ennius: plebes, ait, in hoc regio antistat loco: licet lacrimare plebi, regi honeste non licet. ut regi, sic episcopo, immo minus regi quam episcopo.
passages.english: The poet Naevius says: 'A mortal must suffer many evils.' Hence antiquity also imagined that Niobe, because she wept much, was changed into stone, and [others] into various beasts, as Hecuba into a dog; and Hesiod, lamenting the births of men, rejoices at a funeral. And Ennius wisely says: 'The common people surpass the king in this respect: the people may weep, for a king it is not honourable.' As for a king, so for a bishop; indeed, less for a king than for a bishop.
passages.notes: The parenthesis '(conuersas alias ut Hecubam in canem)' is syntactically awkward and may be a corrupt or interpolated phrase; the Naevius quotation is likely Ennius in other attributions.

passages.original: LXII. AD TRANQVILLINUM, QVOMODO ORIGENEM LEGERE DEBEAMUS.
passages.english: LXII. To Tranquillinus: How We Ought to Read Origen.

passages.original: et quia meae paruitatis quaeris sententiam, utrum secundum fratrem Faustinum penitus respuendus sit an secundum quosdam legendus — ex hac parte ego —, Origenem propter eruditionem sic interdum legendum arbitror, quomodo Tertullianum et Nouatum, Arnobium et Apollinarem et nonnullos ecclesiasticos scriptores Graecos pariter et Latinos, ut bona eorum eligamus uitemusque contraria iuxta apostolum Paulum dicentem: omnia probate.
passages.english: And since you ask the opinion of my humble self, whether Origen should be utterly rejected, as brother Faustinus [holds], or read, as certain others [hold] — I am of this side — I judge that Origen should sometimes be read for his learning, in the same way as Tertullian and Novatus, Arnobius and Apollinaris, and a number of church writers, Greek and Latin alike, so that we may choose what is good in them and avoid the contrary, according to the apostle Paul, who says: "Test all things."
passages.notes: "Novatus" probably refers to Novatian.

passages.original: refert Iosephus — nam aetate eius adhuc templum stabat et necdum Uespasianus et Titus Hierosolymam subuerterant et erat ipse de genere sacerdotali, multoque plus intellegitur, quod oculis uidetur, quam, quod aure percipitur — haec feminalia de bysso retorta ob fortitudinem solere contexi et, postquam incisa fuerint, acu consui;
passages.english: Josephus relates — for in his time the temple was still standing, and Vespasian and Titus had not yet overthrown Jerusalem, and he himself was of priestly family, and much more is understood of what is seen with the eyes than of what is received by the ear — that these breeches were customarily woven of twisted linen for strength, and, after they had been cut, were sewn with a needle;

passages.original: Secunda ex lino tunica est poderes, id est talaris, duplici sindone, quam et ipsam Iosephus byssinam uocat, appellaturque \'cotonat\', id est λιτών, quod Hebraeo sermone in lineam uertitur. haec adhaeret corpori et ita arta est et strictis manicis, ut nulla omnino in ueste sit ruga et usque ad cruraĮ descendat.
passages.english: The second [garment] is a linen tunic, the *poderes* (that is, reaching to the ankles), of double fine linen, which Josephus too calls "of byssus"; and it is called *cotonat*, that is, *chitōn*, which in the Hebrew language is translated "linen [garment]". This clings to the body and is so tight and has such narrow sleeves that there is no fold at all in the garment, and it comes down to the legs.
passages.notes: The Greek printed λιτών is evidently χιτών (chitōn); stray mark after "crura" omitted.

passages.original: praecedebat alios dignitate, sed et alios sequebatur. quamuis clarus honor uilescit in turba et apud bonos uiros indigna ipsa fit dignitas, quam multi indigni possident. unde egregie de Caesare Tullius: dum quosdam, ait, ornare uoluit, non illos honestauit, sed ornamenta ipsa turpauit.
passages.english: He went before others in rank, but he also followed others. Indeed, even illustrious honour grows cheap in a crowd, and among good men rank itself becomes unworthy when many unworthy men possess it. Hence Tully's excellent remark about Caesar: "While he wished to adorn certain men," he says, "he did not dignify them, but disgraced the ornaments themselves."

passages.original: scitum est illud Catonis: sat cito, si sat bene, quod nos quondam adulescentuli, cum a praefecto oratore in praefatiuncula diceretur, risimus. meminisse te puto erroris mutui, quando omne Athenaeum scholasticorum uocibus consonabat: sat cito, si sat bene.
passages.english: Cato's saying is a clever one: "Quick enough, if good enough." We once laughed at it as young men, when it was spoken by a prefect-orator in a little preface. I think you remember our shared error, when the whole Athenaeum resounded with the voices of the students: "Quick enough, if good enough."

passages.original: de radice peruenis ad cacumen; primus inter monachos in prima urbe primum sequeris patriarcham. Loth, quod interpretatur \'declinans\', campestria eligat et iuxta Pythagorae litteram facilia magis et sinistra ac peritura sectetur; tu in arduis et saxosis cum Sarra tibi monumentum para, ut iuxta sit ciuitas litterarum deletisque gigantibus filiis Enac hereditatem tuam gaudium et risus excipiat.
passages.english: From the root you reach the summit; first among monks, in the first city, you follow the first patriarch. Let Lot, whose name means "turning aside", choose the plains, and, according to Pythagoras' letter, pursue what is easier and to the left and doomed to perish; you, in steep and rocky places, prepare a tomb for yourself with Sarah, so that the city of letters may be near, and, the giants, the sons of Anak, having been destroyed, joy and laughter may receive your inheritance.
passages.notes: "Pythagoras' letter" is the letter Y, symbol of the choice between paths. The "city of letters" alludes to Kiriath-sepher near Hebron.

passages.original: \'ornatum\' quoque Izttaatc est prioris uerbi, id est \'inreprehensibilis\'. qui uitia non habet, inreprehensibilis appellatur; qui uirtutibus pollet, ornatus est. possumus et aliud intellegei-e ex hoc uerbo iuxta illud Tullii: \'caput est artis decere, quod facias\'. sunt enim quidam ignorantes mensuram suam et tantae stoliditatis ac uecordiae, ut et in motu et in incessu et in habitu et in sermone communi risum spectantibus tj-ibuant et quasi intellegentes, quid sit ornatus, comant se uestibus et munditiis corporis et lautioris mensae epulas parent, cum omnis istius modi ornatus et cultus sordibus foedior sit.
passages.english: "Ornate" is also an explanation of the preceding word, that is, "irreproachable". One who has no vices is called irreproachable; one who is strong in virtues is ornate. We can also understand something else from this word, according to that saying of Tully: "The chief point of art is that what you do should be becoming." For there are some who are ignorant of their own measure and of such stupidity and folly that in movement, in gait, in dress and in ordinary speech they give onlookers cause for laughter, and, as if they understood what ornament is, they deck themselves out in clothes and bodily elegance and prepare banquets of a more sumptuous table, when all ornament and refinement of this kind is fouler than filth.
passages.notes: "Izttaatc" is a garbled Greek word, probably ἐπεξήγησις or similar ("explanation"); sense conjectural.

passages.original: nec mirum, si apud Latinos metrum non seruet ad uerbum expressa translatio, cum Homerus eadem lingua uersus in prosam uix cohaereat. in alia quoque epistula Menandri ponit senarium: corrumpunt mores bonos confabulationes pessimae. et apud Athenienses in Martis curia disputans Aratum testem uocat: ipsius enim et genus sumus, quod Graece dicitur: tiJijvapϰϰὶ γένος ἐσμέν et est clausula uersus heroici.
passages.english: Nor is it surprising if among the Latins a translation rendered word for word does not keep the metre, since Homer, translated into prose in the same language, scarcely hangs together. In another letter too he quotes a senarius of Menander: "Evil conversations corrupt good morals." And, disputing among the Athenians in the court of Mars, he calls Aratus as witness: "For we are also his offspring," which in Greek is *tou gar kai genos esmen*, and it is the close of a heroic verse.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by scanning; read as τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν. "He" is Paul.

passages.original: Cyprianus, uir et eloquentia pollens et martyrio, Firmiano narrante mordetur, cur aduersus Demetrianum scribens testimoniis usus sit prophetarum et apostolorum, quae ille ficta et commenticia esse ducebat, et non potius philosophorum ac poetarum, quorum auctoritati ut ethnicus contra ire non poterat. scripserunt contra nos Celsus atque Porphyrius: priori Origenes, alteri Methodius, Eusebius et Apollinaris fortissime responderunt.
passages.english: Cyprian, a man eminent both for eloquence and for martyrdom, is criticised, as Firmianus relates, because in writing against Demetrianus he used testimonies of the prophets and apostles, which that man regarded as fictitious and invented, and not rather those of the philosophers and poets, whose authority he, as a pagan, could not oppose. Celsus and Porphyry wrote against us: Origen answered the former, and Methodius, Eusebius and Apollinaris answered the latter most powerfully.
passages.notes: Firmianus is Lactantius (Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius).

passages.original: Clemens, Alexandrinae ecclesiae presbyter, uir meo iudicio omnium eruditissimus, octo scripsit Stromatum libros et totidem Υποτυπώσεων et alium contra gentes, Paedagogi quoque tria uolumina. quid in illis indoctum, immo quid non de media philosophia est? hunc imitatus Origenes decem scripsit Stromateas Christianorum et philosophorum inter se sententias conparans et omnia nostrae religionis dogmata de Platone et Aristotele, Numenio Cornutoque confirmans. scripsit et Miltiades contra gentes uolumen egregium Hippolytusque et Apollonius, Romanae urbis senator, propria opuscula condiderunt.
passages.english: Clement, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, in my judgement the most learned of all men, wrote eight books of Stromata and as many of Hypotyposeis, and another against the pagans, and also three volumes of the Paedagogus. What is there in them that is unlearned, or rather, what is there that is not from the heart of philosophy? Imitating him, Origen wrote ten Stromateis, comparing the opinions of Christians and philosophers with one another and confirming all the doctrines of our religion from Plato and Aristotle, Numenius and Cornutus. Miltiades also wrote an excellent volume against the pagans, and Hippolytus and Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome, composed works of their own.
passages.notes: Hypotyposeis ('Outlines') is given in Greek in the text.

passages.original: Salem autem non, ut Iosephus et nostrorum omnes arbitrantur, esse Hierusalem, nomen ex Graeco Hebraeoque conpositum, quod absurdum esse peregrinae linguae mixtura demonstrat, sed oppidum iuxta Scythopolim, quod usque hodie appellatur Salem.
passages.english: Salem, however, is not Jerusalem, as Josephus and all our [writers] suppose, a name compounded from Greek and Hebrew, which the mixture of a foreign language shows to be absurd, but a town near Scythopolis which is called Salem to this day.

passages.original: refert Irenaeus, uir apostolicorum temporum et Papiae, auditoris euangelistae Iohannis, discipulus episcopusque ecclesiae Lugdunensis, quod Marcus quidam de Basilidis Gnostici stirpe descendens primum ad Gallias uenerit et eas partes, per quas Rodanus et Garunna fluunt, sua doctrina maculauerit maximeque nobiles feminas quaedam in occulto mysteria repromittens hoc errore seduxerit magicis artibus et secreta corporum uoluptate amorem sui concilians, inde Pireneum transiens Spanias occuparit et hoc studii habuerit, ut diuitum domus et in ipsis feminas maxime adpeteret, I quae ducuntur uariis desideriis semper discentes et numquam ad scientiam ueritatis peruenientes.
passages.english: Irenaeus, a man of apostolic times, a disciple of Papias the hearer of John the evangelist, and bishop of the church of Lyons, relates that a certain Marcus, descended from the stock of Basilides the Gnostic, first came to Gaul and stained with his teaching those parts through which the Rhône and the Garonne flow, and above all seduced noble women with this error, promising them certain mysteries in secret, winning their love for himself by magic arts and by the secret pleasure of the body; that then, crossing the Pyrenees, he took over Spain and made it his aim to go after the houses of the rich, and in them especially the women, who are led away by various desires, always learning and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth.
passages.notes: A stray 'I' before 'quae' omitted as a scanning artefact. The final clause quotes 2 Timothy 3:6–7.

passages.original: aberat tunc Romanus exercitus et bellis ciuilibus in Italia tenebatur. hanc gentem Herodotus refert sub Dario, rege Medorum, uiginti annis Orientem tenuisse captiuum et ab Aegyptiis atque Aethiopibus annuum exegisse uectigal. auertat Iesus ab orbe Romano tales ultra bestias! insperati ubique aderant et famam celeritate uincentes non religioni, non dignitatibus, non aetati, non uagienti miserebantur infantiae.
passages.english: The Roman army was absent at that time and was held in Italy by civil wars. Herodotus reports that this nation, under Darius king of the Medes, held the East captive for twenty years and exacted an annual tribute from the Egyptians and Ethiopians. May Jesus turn such beasts away from the Roman world henceforth! They were everywhere unexpectedly present, and outstripping rumour by their speed they had no pity for religion, for rank, for age, or for wailing infancy.

passages.original: in typo horum camelorum Ismahelitae negotiatores stacten et thymiama et resinam, quae nascitur in Galaad et cutem uulneribus obducit, Aegyptiis deferunt tantaeque felicitatis sunt, ut emant et uendant Ioseph et mercimonium eorum salus mundi sit. docet et Aesopi fabula plenum muris uentrem per angustum foramen egredi non ualere.
passages.english: In the figure of these camels the Ishmaelite merchants carry to the Egyptians myrrh-oil and incense and resin, which grows in Gilead and closes the skin over wounds; and they are of such good fortune that they buy and sell Joseph, and their merchandise is the salvation of the world. Aesop's fable also teaches that a mouse with a full belly cannot get out through a narrow hole.
passages.notes: 'stacten': stacte, oil of myrrh (cf. Genesis 37:25).

passages.original: Scio quam plurimos fratrum scientiae scripturarum desiderio prouocatos poposcisse ab aliquantis eruditis uiris et Graecarum peritis, ut Origenem Romanum facerent et Latinis auribus * eum donarent. in quod etiam cum frater et collega noster ab episcopo Damaso deprecatus homilias duas de Cantico canticorum in Latinum transtulisset ex Graeco, ita in illo opere ornate magnificeque praefatus est, ut cuiuis legendi Origenem et auidissime perquirendi desiderium commoueret, dicens illius animae conuenire, quod dictum est, quia introduxit me rex in cubiculum suum, adserens eum, quod, cum in ceteris libris omnes uincat, in Canticis canticorum etiam ipse se uicerit.
passages.english: I know that very many of the brothers, stirred by a desire for knowledge of the Scriptures, have asked a number of learned men skilled in Greek to make Origen Roman and present him to Latin ears. When to this end our brother and colleague, at the request of Bishop Damasus, had also translated two homilies on the Song of Songs from Greek into Latin, he wrote so elegant and splendid a preface to that work that it would stir in anyone a desire to read Origen and seek him out most eagerly, saying that what was said, 'the king has brought me into his chamber', fits his soul, and asserting that, while he surpasses everyone in his other books, in the Song of Songs he surpassed even himself.
passages.notes: An asterisk in the text (after 'auribus') marks a possible lacuna or editorial note; nothing seems missing in sense. The 'brother and colleague' is Jerome.

passages.original: cuius diuersitatis causam plenius tibi in Apologetico, quem Pamphilus pro libris ipsius Origenis scripsit, edidimus breuissimo libello superaddito, in quo euidentibus, ut arbitror, probamentis corruptos esse in quam plurimis ab hereticis et maliuolis libros eius ostendimus et praecipue istos, quos nunc exigis ut interpreter, id est περὶ ἀρχῶν, quod uel \'de principiis\' uel \'de principatibus\' dici potest, qui sunt re uera alias et obscurissimi et difficillimi.
passages.english: The cause of this discrepancy I have set out for you more fully in the Apology which Pamphilus wrote for the books of Origen himself, adding a very short booklet, in which I have shown by, as I think, clear proofs that his books have been corrupted in very many places by heretics and ill-wishers, and especially these which you now require me to translate, that is Peri archōn, which can be rendered either 'On First Principles' or 'On Principalities', which are in truth otherwise both extremely obscure and extremely difficult.
passages.notes: Probably Rufinus's preface rather than Jerome's.

passages.original: et beatus Cyprianus Tertulliano magistro utitur, ut eius scripta probant; cumque eruditi et ardentis uiri delectetur ingenio, Montanum cum eo Maximillamque non sequitur. fortissimos libros contra J Porphyrium scripsit Apollinaris, ecclesiasticam pulchre Eusebius i historiam texuit; alter eorum dimidiatam Christi introducit οἰκονομίαν, alter inpietatis Arrii apertissimus propugnator est:
passages.english: And blessed Cyprian uses Tertullian as his teacher, as his writings prove; and although he delights in the genius of that learned and ardent man, he does not follow him with Montanus and Maximilla. Apollinaris wrote very powerful books against Porphyry; Eusebius composed a fine ecclesiastical history; one of them introduces a halved oikonomia [dispensation, i.e. incarnation] of Christ, the other is a most open champion of the impiety of Arius.
passages.notes: Stray letters 'J' and 'i' omitted as scanning artefacts.

passages.original: ex quo intellegi uolunt nos, qui necdum initiati sumus, debere audire mendacium, ne paruuli atque lactantes solidioris cibi edulio suffocemur. quod autem periuriorum atque mendacii inter se orgiis foederentur, sextus Stromatum liber, in quo Platonis sententiae nostrum dogma conponit, planissime docet.
passages.english: From this they want it understood that we, who are not yet initiated, ought to hear a lie, so that as little ones and sucklings we may not be choked by a meal of more solid food. And that they are bound together among themselves by rites of perjury and lying, the sixth book of the Stromata, in which [Origen] compares Plato's opinions with our doctrine, teaches most plainly.
passages.notes: 'conponit' taken as 'compares' (cf. 'conparans' elsewhere); the subject of the Stromata here is presumably Origen.

passages.original: quis mihi interdicere potest, ne legam Institutionum eius libros, quibus contra gentes scripsit fortissime, quia superior sententia detestanda est? Apollinaris contra Porphyrium egregia scribit uolumina: probo laborem uiri, licet fatuum in plerisque dogma contemnam. confitemini et uos in quibusdam errasse Origenem, et muttum non faciam.
passages.english: Who can forbid me to read his books of the Institutes, in which he wrote most powerfully against the pagans, because the opinion above is to be detested? Apollinaris writes excellent volumes against Porphyry: I approve the man's labour, although I despise his foolish doctrine in many points. Do you too confess that Origen erred in certain things, and I will not say a word.
passages.notes: 'his' refers presumably to Lactantius (Divine Institutes), named outside the passage.

passages.original: Uult aliquis laudare Origenem? laudet, ut laudo: magnus uir ab infantia et uere martyris filius Alexandriae ecclesiasticam scholam tenuit succedens eruditissimo uiro, Clementi presbytero; uoluptates in tantum fugiit, ut zelo dei, sed non secundum scientiam ferro truncaret genitalia;
passages.english: Does anyone want to praise Origen? Let him praise [him], as I praise [him]: a great man from his childhood, and truly the son of a martyr, he headed the church's school at Alexandria, succeeding that most learned man, Clement the presbyter; he fled pleasures to such a degree that, out of zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, he cut off his genitals with a blade;

passages.original: solus scilicet inuentus est Origenes, cuius scripta in toto orbe pariter falsarentur et quasi ad Mithridatis litteras omnis ueritas uno die de uoluminibus illius raderetur. si unus uiolatus est liber, num uniuersa eius opera, quae diuersis et locis et temporibus edidit, simul corrumpi potuerunt? ipse Origenes in epistula, quam scribit ad Fabianum, Romanae urbis episcopum, paenitentiam agit, cur talia scripserit, et causas temeritatis in Ambrosium refert, quod secreto edita in publicum protulerit: et quidam adhuc svQsoihoyovoiv aliena esse, quae displicent!
passages.english: Origen alone, it seems, has been found whose writings were falsified equally throughout the whole world, and from whose volumes all truth was erased in a single day, as if by the letters of Mithridates. If one book was tampered with, could all his works, which he published in different places and at different times, have been corrupted at once? Origen himself, in the letter which he writes to Fabian, bishop of the city of Rome, does penance for having written such things, and lays the blame for his rashness on Ambrose, because he brought out in public what had been put out privately: and yet some still [...] that the things which displease are someone else's!
passages.notes: "svQsoihoyovoiv" is a garbled Greek word from the scan; it is probably a form of a Greek verb meaning roughly 'maintain' or 'reason plausibly'. The exact reading is uncertain, so it is left untranslated. "Mithridates' letters" refers to his orders for a massacre on a single day.

passages.original: ecce uos emendatis in Origenis libris, quod ille non scripsit, et miramini, si edat aliquis librum, quem ille non edidit? uos in edito opere potestis coargui; ille, qui nihil aliud edidit, facilius patet calumniae. date quodlibet aliud opus Pamphili, nusquam repperietis;
passages.english: Look, you correct in Origen's books what he did not write, and are you surprised if someone publishes a book that he did not publish? You can be refuted from a published work; he, who published nothing else, lies more open to false accusation. Produce any other work of Pamphilus; you will find none anywhere;

passages.original: sex librorum Eusebii super Origenis defensione principium usque ad mille ferme uersus liber iste, qui Pamphili dicitur, continet et in reliquis scriptor eiusdem operis profert testimonia, quibus nititur adprobare Origenem fuisse catholicum. Eusebius et Pamphilus tantam inter se habuere concordiam, ut unius animae homines putes et ab uno alter nomen acceperit. quomodo igitur inter se dissentire potuerunt, ut Eusebius in toto opere suo Origenem Arriani dogmatis probet et Pamphilus Niccenae k. synodi, quae fuit postea, defensorem? ex quo ostenditur uel Didymi, uel cuiuslibet alterius esse opusculum, qui sex librorum capiti detrun- i cato cetera membra sociarit.
passages.english: This book, which is said to be Pamphilus', contains the beginning of Eusebius' six books in defence of Origen, up to nearly a thousand lines, and in the rest the writer of that same work produces testimonies by which he tries to prove that Origen was catholic. Eusebius and Pamphilus had such harmony between them that you would think them men of one soul, and the one took his name from the other. How then could they disagree with each other, so that Eusebius in his whole work proves Origen [a holder] of the Arian doctrine, and Pamphilus [proves him] a defender of the Nicene synod, which came later? From this it is shown that the little work is either Didymus' or someone else's, who cut off the head of the six books and joined the remaining limbs together.
passages.notes: "Niccenae k." and "detrun- i cato" contain scanning debris; read as "Nicaenae" and "detruncato".

passages.original: Primae in libris ffteoldoxcbv, quos nuper Pammachio nostro iubente interpretatus sum, Origenes fortissime respondit; quo detentus opere inplere non potui, quod tibi promiseram, et Danielem nostrum rursum conperendinaui. et quidem, quamuis mei amantissimi et egregii uiri, tamen unius uoluntatem in tempus aliud distulissem, nisi omnis paene fraternitas de urbe eadem postulasset adserens multos periclitari et peruersis dogmatibus adquiescere.
passages.english: Origen gave his strongest answer in the first [book] of the books *Peri Archōn* (On First Principles), which I recently translated at the bidding of our Pammachius; held up by this work, I could not fulfil what I had promised you, and I have once more postponed our Daniel. And indeed, though [he is] a most loving and excellent man to me, I would still have put off the wish of one man to another time, had not almost the whole brotherhood of that same city demanded it, asserting that many were in danger and were assenting to perverse doctrines.
passages.notes: "ffteoldoxcbv" is a garbled scan, presumably for Greek Περὶ ἀρχῶν. The opening "Primae" is uncertain; it may refer to the first [questions] rather than the first book.

passages.original: Praeterea, quia docto uiro loquor et tam diuinis scripturis quam saeculi litteris erudito, illud dignationem tuam admonitam uolo, ne me putes in modum rustici balatronis cuncta Origenis reprobare, quae scripsit - quod in me criminantur ἀκαιροσπουδασταὶ eius et quasi Dionysium philosophum arguunt subito mutasse sententiam —, sed tantum praua dogmata repudiare.
passages.english: Moreover, since I am speaking to a learned man, educated both in the divine scriptures and in secular literature, I want your worthiness to be advised not to think that, in the manner of a rustic buffoon, I reject everything Origen wrote (which his ill-timed zealots charge against me, accusing me, like the philosopher Dionysius, of having suddenly changed my opinion), but [that I] only repudiate his depraved doctrines.
passages.notes: Dionysius is presumably Dionysius 'the Renegade' of Heraclea, a Stoic who turned Epicurean.

passages.original: Dolent contra me atque insaniunt, quare solitudines et habitacula monachorum, in quibus sancta conuersatio est, non .\' permiserim inpiis Origenis dogmatibus pollui. e quibus ut cetera praetermittam, in libris Resurrectionis, quos scripsit ad Ambrosium dialecticum morem imitans disputandi, in quo sciscitatus est atque responsio, artis magicae praedicator his uerbis est: ars magica non mihi uidetur alicuius rei subsistentis uocabulum, sed et, si sit, nequaquam est operis mali nec quod haberi possit contemptui.
passages.english: They grieve and rage against me because I did not allow the solitudes and dwellings of the monks, in which there is holy living, to be polluted by Origen's impious doctrines. Of these, to pass over the rest: in the books *On the Resurrection*, which he wrote to Ambrose, imitating the dialectical manner of disputing, with question and answer, he is a preacher of the magic art in these words: "The magic art does not seem to me the name of anything subsisting, but even if it were, it is by no means a work of evil, nor something that could be held in contempt."
passages.notes: Stray characters ".\'" before "permiserim" omitted.

passages.original: et docere nos cupiens, quod et pater m tiiio et filius in patre creaturis omnibus imperaret, et hoc ipsum roborans inferebat: ego et pater unum sumus, ne quis unum suum patrisque regnum humanae carnis occasione diuideret. quodsi iuxta Origenis insaniam aliquando amissurus est regnum Christus, unigenitus filius dei, quomodo ipse apostolis loquebatur: ego et pater unum sumus, non unum postea habiturus imperium, ut scilicet hic habeat gloriam, quam ibi depositurus est?
passages.english: And, wishing to teach us that both the father in the son and the son in the father rule over all creatures, and confirming this very point, he added: "I and the Father are one," so that no one might divide his and the Father's one kingdom on account of the human flesh. But if, according to Origen's madness, Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, is at some time going to lose the kingdom, how did he himself say to the apostles, "I and the Father are one," if he is not afterwards going to have one rule, so that he has here a glory that he is going to lay down there?
passages.notes: "m tiiio" is a garbled scan, probably "in filio" (in the son), which fits the sense; the text may be corrupt.

passages.original: Itaque nulli dubium est, quin, qui deus permanet in aeternum, simul habeat et regnum et super ipsos quoque, quos regni possessione donauit, rex perpetuus appelletur congruum habens diuinitatis imperium nec quicquam in se rude et nouum nisi adsumptionem fragilitatis humanae. si enim iuxta Origenis insaniam post multorum circulos saeculorum Christi regnum est finiendum, consequens inpietati eius est dicere, ut et deus esse aliquando desistat; et, qui regni terminos ponit, cogitur idem de diuinitate sentire, quae perpetuitatem imperii naturaliter possidet.
passages.english: Therefore no one doubts that he who remains God forever has also the kingdom together [with it], and is called eternal king even over those whom he has gifted with possession of the kingdom, having a rule befitting his divinity, and nothing in himself crude and new except the assumption of human frailty. For if, according to Origen's madness, Christ's kingdom is to be ended after the cycles of many ages, it follows from his impiety to say that he will also at some time cease to be God; and whoever sets limits to the kingdom is forced to think the same about the divinity, which by nature possesses perpetuity of rule.

passages.original: quod et magi intellegentes uersi ad paenitentiam studiosius percunctabantur: ubi est, qui natus est rex Iudaeorum? uidimus enim stellam eius in oriente et uenimus, ut adoremus eum. magi fatentur Christum regem et Origenes negat dicens eum non in perpetuo regnaturum nec animaduertit se Iudaeorum blasphemiis similem. t
passages.english: Understanding this, the magi too, turned to repentance, inquired more eagerly: "Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east and have come to worship him." The magi confess Christ as king, and Origen denies it, saying that he will not reign forever, and he does not notice that he is like the Jews in their blasphemies.
passages.notes: Stray final "t" omitted.

passages.original: neque enim, quos semel saluos fecit, iterum praecipitabit e caelo et dimittet iuxta Origenis deliramenta et fabulas, ut rursum de sublimibus conruant. et hoc, quod dicitur: non uidebis utra mala, aeternae securitatis indicium est, quod, qui semel fuerint liberati et regni caelorum possessione perfruiti, nequaquam uitiis trahantur ad terram nec dei priuentur auxilio, qui eis iuxta eloquium prophetale ponet murum et circamurale sua eos uirtute circumdans.
passages.english: For those whom he has once saved he will not again cast headlong from heaven and let go, according to the ravings and fables of Origen, so that they fall down once more from the heights. And this saying, "You will not see either of the evils," is a sign of eternal security: that those who have once been set free and have enjoyed possession of the kingdom of heaven are by no means dragged down to earth by vices, nor deprived of the help of God, who, according to the prophet's word, will set for them a wall and an outer wall, surrounding them with his power.
passages.notes: "non uidebis utra mala": the scriptural source is uncertain; the sense of "utra" ("either/both") is unclear.

passages.original: Uerum quid ista memoramus, cum in tantam eruperit uecordiam, immo dementiam, ut aliud saluatori crimen inpingat dicens eum et pro daemonibus ac spiritalibus nequitiis apud superos adfigendum cruci ? nec intellegit, in quam profundum inpietatis conruat barathrum. si enim Christus pro hominibus passus homo factus est, ut scripturarum testantur eloquia, consequens erit, ut dicat Origenes: \'et pro daemonibus passurus daemon futurus est\'. hoc enim necessitate cogetur ut inferat, ne ab eo, quod coepit, discrepare uideatur et ut imitetur blasphemias Iudaeorum, quos semper imitatur; et illi enim Christo similiter loquebantur: daemonium habes et: in Belzebul, principe daemoniorum, eicis daemonia.
passages.english: But why do we mention these things, when he has burst out into such madness, or rather insanity, that he lays another charge against the Saviour, saying that he must also be fastened to a cross in the heavenly places for the demons and the spiritual forces of wickedness? Nor does he understand into what deep pit of impiety he is plunging. For if Christ, in order to suffer for human beings, became a human being, as the words of the Scriptures testify, it will follow that Origen should say: 'And in order to suffer for demons he will become a demon.' For he will be forced by necessity to draw this conclusion, so as not to seem to depart from what he began, and so as to imitate the blasphemies of the Jews, whom he always imitates; for they too spoke similarly to Christ: "You have a demon," and: "By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, you cast out demons."

passages.original: Unde liberati a cunctis malis passionis dominicae festa celebremus et iuxta euangelii parabolam cernentes a sapientia immolari tauros et altilia uescamur fortioribus plenisque neruorum et pinguioribus doctrinae cibis, ut lac infantiae deserentes solidiora capiamus alimenta causamque malorum omnium fugiamus inperitiam, quae, cum multorum diuersis heresibus uinxerit pedes, Origene maximo sui fruitur amatore, qui inter cetera ausus est dicere non esse orandum filium neque cum filio patrem ac post multa saecula Pharaonis instaurauit blasphemiam dicentis: quis est, ut audiam uocem eius? nescio dominum et Israhel non dimittam. nec est aliud dicere \'nescio dominum\' quam hoc, quod dicit Origenes: \'non est orandus filius\', quem certe dominum confitetur.
passages.english: Therefore, set free from all evils, let us celebrate the feast of the Lord's passion, and, seeing according to the Gospel parable that bulls and fatlings are sacrificed by Wisdom, let us feed on the stronger, sinewy and richer foods of doctrine, so that, leaving behind the milk of infancy, we may take more solid nourishment and flee ignorance, the cause of all evils; which, though it has bound the feet of many with various heresies, enjoys in Origen its greatest lover, who among other things dared to say that the Son is not to be prayed to, nor the Father together with the Son, and after many ages revived the blasphemy of Pharaoh, who said: "Who is he, that I should hear his voice? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." And to say 'I do not know the Lord' is nothing other than what Origen says: 'The Son is not to be prayed to', whom he certainly confesses to be Lord.

passages.original: itaque nec deum credit Origenes filium dei, quem non putat adorandum, et lacerat eum conuiciis; cumque sibi in scripturarum memoria blandiatur et putet se eas intellegere, non audit contra se loquentem Moysen: homo, qui maledixerit deum, peccatum habebit et, qui nominauerit nomen domini, morte morietur; lapidibus obruet eum omnis multitudo. et quis tantis Christum adficit contumeliis ut hic, qui ausus est dicere: \'non debet orari\' cassum tantum ei diuinitatis nomen indulgens?
passages.english: So Origen does not believe that the Son of God is God, since he does not think he should be worshipped, and he tears him with insults; and though he flatters himself on his memory of the Scriptures and thinks he understands them, he does not hear Moses speaking against him: "The man who curses God shall bear sin, and he who names the name of the Lord shall surely die; the whole multitude shall overwhelm him with stones." And who heaps such insults on Christ as this man, who dared to say: 'He ought not to be prayed to', granting him only an empty name of divinity?
passages.notes: "nominauerit" reflects the Septuagint sense of 'naming' (i.e. blaspheming) the name of the Lord.

passages.original: si enim incorruptio corpora in nihilum redigit, consequens fuerat dicere corruptioni ea in perpetuum reseruari essetque fortior incorruptione. sed absit Paulum contraria sibi scribere et incorruptioni et corruptioni eandem esse naturam. quodsi, ut falso putat Origenes, non solum corruptibile, sed et mortale corpus i est suscitandum, ergo unum atque idem corruptio et incorruptio,, mors et uita dicentur; eandem habebunt in suscitatis corporibus potestatem et nequaquam rebus, sed tantum nominibus corruptio et incorruptio, mors et uita separabuntur.
passages.english: For if incorruption reduces bodies to nothing, it would have followed to say that they are preserved for ever for corruption, and [corruption] would be stronger than incorruption. But far be it that Paul should write things contrary to himself, and that incorruption and corruption should have the same nature. But if, as Origen falsely thinks, not only the corruptible but also the mortal body is to be raised, then corruption and incorruption, death and life, will be called one and the same; they will have the same power in the raised bodies, and corruption and incorruption, death and life, will be distinguished not in reality at all but only in names.
passages.notes: Stray letter "i" after "corpus" omitted as a scanning artefact.

passages.original: nam si natura corporea uana est et futilis iuxta Origenis errorem, cur Christus surrexit a mortuis, quare nostra corpora suscitauit, quid sibi uult Paulus scribens: s i mortui non resurgent, nec Christus resurrexit; si autem Christus non resurrexit, uana est fides nostra?
passages.english: For if bodily nature is empty and worthless, according to Origen's error, why did Christ rise from the dead, why did he raise our bodies, what does Paul mean when he writes: "If the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen; but if Christ has not risen, our faith is vain"?

passages.original: cessent Apollinaris discipuli ea, quae contra ecclesiasticas regulas est locutus, propter alia eius scripta defendere. licet enim aduersus Arrianos et Eunomianos scripserit et Origenem aliosque hereticos sua disputatione subuerterit, tamen, qui memor est illius praecepti: non accipies personam in iudicio, ueritatem semper debet diligere, non personas, et scire, quod in dispensatione hominis, quem pro salute nostra unigenitus filius dei est dignatus adsumere, non sit alienus a culpa, qui super anima illius peruersa et intellexit et scripsit.
passages.english: Let the disciples of Apollinaris cease defending, on account of his other writings, the things he said against the rules of the Church. For although he wrote against the Arians and Eunomians and overthrew Origen and other heretics by his argument, nevertheless whoever remembers that precept, "You shall not show partiality in judgment," ought always to love the truth, not persons, and to know that, concerning the economy of the humanity which the only-begotten Son of God deigned to assume for our salvation, he is not free from blame who both understood and wrote perversely about his soul.
passages.notes: "dispensatione" renders the theological term oikonomia (economy of the incarnation).

passages.original: Unde sciendum est, quod ex omni parte temperatum humanae condicionis exhibens sacramentum perfectam similitudinem nostrae condicionis adsumpserit nec carnem tantum nec animam inrationalem et sine sensu, sed totum corpus totamque animam sibi socians perfectum in se hominem demonstrarit, ut perfectam cunctis hominibus in se et per se largiretur salutem; habensque nostri consortium, qui de terra conditi sumus, nec carnem deduxit de caelo nec animam, quae prius substiterat et ante carnem eius condita erat, suo corpori copulauit, sicut Origenis nituntur docere discipuli.
passages.english: Hence it must be known that, displaying the mystery of the human condition balanced in every respect, he assumed the perfect likeness of our condition, neither flesh alone nor an irrational soul without sense, but, uniting to himself a whole body and a whole soul, he showed forth a perfect man in himself, so that in himself and through himself he might bestow perfect salvation on all people; and, having fellowship with us who were formed from earth, he neither brought flesh down from heaven nor joined to his body a soul that had previously existed and had been created before his flesh, as the disciples of Origen strive to teach.

passages.original: Quae enim illum ratio, qui disputationum ordo perduxit, ut allegoriae umbris et cassis imaginibus scripturarum tolleret ueritatem? quis propheta sentire docuit ob lapsus de caelis animarum deum esse conpulsum corpora fabricare ? quis iuxta beatum Lucam eorum, qui uiderunt et ministri fuerunt sermonis dei, huic tradidit ad docendum neglegentia et motu et fluxu de altioribus rationabilium creaturarum prouocatum deum mundi huius condere diuersitatem, cum creationem eius Moyses explicans (nec) dixerit nec indicauerit propter causas aliquas praecedentes de rationabilibus\' sensibilia, de inuisibilibus uisibilia, de melioribus peiora prolata, quod apertissime Origenes praedicat?
passages.english: For what reasoning, what sequence of arguments led him to take away the truth of the Scriptures by the shadows of allegory and empty images? What prophet taught him to think that God was compelled to fashion bodies because of the fall of souls from heaven? Which of those who, according to blessed Luke, were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word of God handed on to him for teaching that God, provoked by the negligence, movement and downward flowing of rational creatures from higher states, founded the diversity of this world, when Moses, in setting out its creation, neither said nor indicated that, because of some preceding causes, sensible things were produced from rational ones, visible from invisible, worse from better, which Origen most openly proclaims?
passages.notes: The bracketed "(nec)" is an editorial supplement; stray apostrophe after "rationabilibus" ignored.

passages.original: et qui iactat se m scientia scripturarum et putat tanta legisse, quanta nullus hominum legerit, sciat scriptum, quod aegrotantes in lectulis deferebant et ponebant in triuiis et plateis, ut Petri eos umbra contingeret et sanaret; quod sacra apostolorum Acta testantur i arguentia Origenis stultitiam, per quae id apostolorum umbra fecisse\' conuincitur, quod ille filium et uerbum dei non potuisse testatur.,
passages.english: And let him who boasts of his knowledge of the Scriptures and thinks he has read as much as no other person has read know that it is written that they carried the sick on beds and laid them at crossroads and in the streets, so that Peter's shadow might touch them and heal them; this the sacred Acts of the Apostles testify, exposing Origen's folly, since by them it is proved that the shadow of the apostles did what he declares the Son and Word of God could not do.
passages.notes: Stray letters ("m" read as "in", "i") and punctuation treated as scanning artefacts.

passages.original: si enlm anima saluatoris est, quae fuit in forma dei et aequalis deo, iuxta Origenis insaniam, aequalis \' autem deo filius dei est et, quod aequale deo est, eiusdem con-\' uincitur esse substantiae, ipse nos disputationis ordo perducit, ut unius naturae animam et deum esse credamus.
passages.english: For if it is the Saviour's soul which was in the form of God and equal to God, according to Origen's madness, and yet the one equal to God is the Son of God, and what is equal to God is shown to be of the same substance, the very sequence of the argument leads us to believe that the soul and God are of one nature.
passages.notes: 'enlm' read as 'enim'; stray marks and the split 'con- uincitur' corrected.

passages.original: si omnes gentes quasi stillae de situla et quasi i momentum staterae reputatae sunt et quasi saliua reputabuntur — per quae uerba omnium creaturarum uilitas et parua substantia demonstratur, ut appareat inconparabilis sublimitas dei —, ergo et fortitudo eius sicut stilla de situla et sicut momentum staterae et saliua hominis reputabitur, si iuxta Origenem tanta fabricatus est, quanta poterat sua uirtute conprehendere, et necesse est numero mensuraeque factorum dei fortitudinem coaequari, si tamen non potuit facere maiora, quam fecit.
passages.english: If all the nations have been reckoned as drops from a bucket and as the turn of the scale, and will be reckoned as spittle (by which words the worthlessness and slight substance of all creatures is shown, so that the incomparable loftiness of God may appear), then his strength too will be reckoned as a drop from a bucket, as the turn of the scale and as a man's spittle, if, according to Origen, he fashioned as many things as he was able to comprehend by his power. Then the strength of God must be made equal to the number and measure of the things he made, if indeed he could not make greater things than he did.
passages.notes: Stray 'i' before 'momentum' omitted. The allusion is to Isaiah 40:15.

passages.original: nec tam stultus sum, ut diuersitate explanationum tuarum me laedi putem, quia nec tu laederis, si nos contraria senserimus. sed illa est uera inter amicos reprehensio, si nostram peram non uidentes aliorum iuxta Persium manticam consideremus.
passages.english: Nor am I so foolish as to think myself injured by the differences between your interpretations and mine, since you are not injured either if we hold contrary views. But the true reproach between friends is this: if, not seeing our own wallet, we look at the knapsack of others, as Persius puts it.

passages.original: Hanc autem expositionem, quam primus Origenes in decimo Stromatum libro, ubi epistulam Pauli ad Galatas interpretatur, et ceteri deinceps interpretes sunt secuti, illa uel maxime causa subintroducunt, ut Porphyrio respondeant blasphemanti, qui Pauli arguit procacitatem, quod principem apostolorum Petrum ausus sit reprehendere et arguere in faciem ac ratione constringere, quod male fecerit, id est in eo errore fuerit, in quo fuit ipse, qui alium -arguit delinquentem.
passages.english: This interpretation, which Origen first [gave] in the tenth book of the Stromateis, where he interprets Paul's letter to the Galatians, and which the other interpreters then followed, they bring in chiefly for this reason: to answer the blasphemous Porphyry. Porphyry charges Paul with impudence, because he dared to rebuke Peter, the chief of the apostles, to reprove him to his face and to pin him down by argument for having done wrong, that is, for being in the very error in which he himself was, who reproved another for going astray.

passages.original: super quo quamuis superior Acacii disputatio plenius uentilarit, tamen dicendum est, quid uideatur aliis, Theodoro uidelicet, Apollinari et Diodoro, qui unam sequuntur sententiam. quorum Diodorus haec scripsit: \'residuos atque uiuentes Paulus apostolus uocat, non quo uelit intellegi et se et alios resurrectionis tempore in corpore repperiendos, sed \'nos\' dixit pro eo, quod est \'iustos, de quorum et ego sum numero\'. ipsi enim rapientur obuiam Christo et non peccatores.
passages.english: Although the earlier discussion of Acacius has aired this question more fully, still I must say what others think, namely Theodore, Apollinaris and Diodorus, who follow one opinion. Of these Diodorus wrote this: 'The apostle Paul calls [them] "those who are left" and "living", not because he wishes it to be understood that he and others would be found in the body at the time of the resurrection, but he said "we" in place of "the righteous, of whose number I too am". For they will be caught up to meet Christ, and not sinners.
passages.notes: Refers to 1 Thessalonians 4:15–17.

passages.original: Haec celeri sermone dictaui, quid eruditi uiri de utroque sentirent loco et quibus argumentis suas uellent probare sententias, uestrae prudentiae exponens. neque enim tanta est meae pusillitatis auctoritas, qui nihil sum et inuidorum tantum morsibus pateo, quanta eorum, qui nos in domino praecesserunt, nec iuxta Pythagorae discipulos praeiudicata doctoris opinio, sed doctrinae ratio ponderanda est.
passages.english: I have dictated this in hasty speech, setting out for your prudence what learned men thought about each passage and by what arguments they wished to prove their opinions. For the authority of my littleness, who am nothing and lie open only to the bites of the envious, is not as great as that of those who went before us in the Lord. Nor, as with the disciples of Pythagoras, is the teacher's opinion to be taken as already decided; rather, the reasoning of the teaching must be weighed.

passages.original: primumque dicendum, quod diuinae potentiae indicium sit ponere animam, quando uoluerit, et rursum accipere eam. denique centurio uidens eum dixisse ad patrem: in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum et statim sponte spiritum dimisisse commotus signi magnitudine ait: uere dei filius erat iste. uelum quoque templi scissum est in duas partes, ut conpleretur id, quod refert Iosephus praesides templi dixisse uirtutes: \'transeamus ex his sedibus\'. in euangelio autem, quod Hebraicis litteris scriptum est, legimus non uelum templi scissum, sed superliminare templi mirae magnitudinis conruisse.
passages.english: First it must be said that it is a sign of divine power to lay down one's soul when one wills and to take it up again. And so the centurion, seeing that he had said to the Father, 'Into your hands I commend my spirit', and had at once given up his spirit of his own accord, was moved by the greatness of the sign and said, 'Truly this was the Son of God.' The veil of the temple too was torn in two, so that what Josephus reports might be fulfilled, that the powers presiding over the temple had said, 'Let us depart from these seats.' But in the gospel written in Hebrew letters we read not that the veil of the temple was torn, but that the lintel of the temple, of wondrous size, collapsed.

passages.original: nobis autem nihil placet, nisi quod ecclesiasticum est et publice in ecclesia dicere non timemus, ne iuxta Pythagoram et Platonem et discipulos eorum, qui sub nomine Christiano introducunt dogma gentilium, dicamus animas lapsas esse de caelo et pro diuersitate meritorum in his uel illis corporibus poenas antiquorum luere peccatorum.
passages.english: But nothing pleases us except what belongs to the Church and what we are not afraid to say publicly in church. [We will] not, following Pythagoras and Plato and their disciples, who under the Christian name bring in the doctrine of the pagans, say that souls fell from heaven and, according to the diversity of their merits, pay in these or those bodies the penalties of ancient sins.

passages.original: olxovofioo, autem tam pecuniae quam frugum et omnium, quae dominus possidet, dispensator est. unde et Olxovojnixog Xenofontis pulcherrimus liber est, qui non gubernationem uillae, sed dispensationem uniuersae domus Tullio interpretante significat.
passages.english: An *oikonomos* [steward], however, is the dispenser of money as well as of crops and of everything the master possesses. Hence Xenophon's *Oikonomikos* is a most beautiful book, which, as Tullius translates it, signifies not the management of a farm but the administration of the whole household.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by scanning ('olxovofioo', 'Olxovojnixog'); read as οἰκονόμος and Οἰκονομικός.

passages.original: haec dicimus non separantes legem et euangelium, ut Marcion calumniatur, sed unum atque eundem suscipientes deum, qui pro uarietate temporum atque causarum principio et fini serit, ut metat, plantat, ut habeat, quod succidat, iacit fundamentum, ut aedificio consummato culmen inponat.
passages.english: We say this not separating the Law and the Gospel, as Marcion falsely charges, but accepting one and the same God, who, according to the variety of times and circumstances, at beginning and end sows that he may reap, plants that he may have something to cut down, lays a foundation that, when the building is completed, he may set the roof on it.

passages.original: In secundo autem libro mundos adserit innumerabiles, non iuxta Epicurum uno tempore plurimos et sui similes, sed post alterius mundi finem alterius esse principium et ante hunc nostrum mundum alium fuisse mundum et post hunc alium rursum futurum et post illum alium rursumque ceteros post ceteros.
passages.english: In the second book he asserts innumerable worlds: not, as Epicurus held, many at one time and like one another, but that after the end of one world there is the beginning of another. Before this world of ours there was another world, and after this one there will again be another, and after that another, and again others after others.
passages.notes: The subject is presumably Origen (De principiis).

passages.original: et iterum: nisi forte corpus hoc pingue atque terrenum caligo et tenebrae nominandae sunt, per quod consummato hoc mundo, cui necesse fuerit in alium transire mundum, rursum nascendi sumet exordia. haec dicens perspicue μετεμψύχσιν Pythagorae Platonisque defendit.
