passages.english: And again: "Unless perhaps this fat and earthly body is to be called mist and darkness, through which, when this world has been brought to its end, whoever must pass into another world will once more take up the beginnings of being born." In saying this he plainly defends the metempsychosis of Pythagoras and Plato.
passages.notes: The Greek is misprinted as μετεμψύχσιν; read μετεμψύχωσιν (transmigration of souls). The speaker is not identified in the passage, presumably Origen.

passages.original: Dum essem iuuenis et solitudinis me deserta uallarent, incentiua uitiorum ardoremque naturae ferre non poteram; quae cum crebris ieiuniis frangerem, mens tamen cogitationibus aestuabat. ad quam edomandam cuidam fratri, qui ex Hebraeis crediderat, me in disciplinam dedi, ut post Quintiliani acumina Ciceronisque fluuios grauitatemque Frontonis et lenitatem Plinii alphabetum discerem, stridentia anhelantiaque uerba meditarer.
passages.english: When I was a young man and the wastes of the desert walled me in, I could not bear the incitements of vice and the heat of nature. Though I broke these with frequent fasts, my mind still seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I put myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had come to believe from among the Hebrews, so that after the sharpness of Quintilian, the rivers of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto and the smoothness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practise hissing and breathy words.

passages.original: super animae statu memini uestrae quaestiunculae, immo maximae ecclesiasticae quaestionis, utrum lapsa de caelo sit, ut Pythagoras philosophus omnesque Platonici et Origenes putant, an dsiOQVOia dei substantiae, ut Stoici, Manicheus et Hispana Priscilliani heresis suspicantur, an in thesauro habeantur dei olim conditae, ut quidam ecclesiastici stulta persuasione confidunt, an cotidie a deo fiant et mittantur in corpora secundum illud, quod in euangelio scriptum est: pater meus usque modo operatur et ego operor, an certe ex traduce, ut Tertullianus, Apollinaris et maxima pars occidentalium autumat, ut, quomodo corpus ex corpore, sic anima nascatur ex anima et simili cum brutis animantibus condicione subsistat.
passages.english: On the state of the soul, I remember your little question, or rather the greatest question of the Church. Has it fallen from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists and Origen think? Or is it an emanation of God's substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian suspect? Or are souls kept in God's treasury, created long ago, as certain churchmen confidently hold in a foolish conviction? Or are they made by God each day and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the gospel: "My Father is working until now, and I am working"? Or, finally, do they come by transmission (ex traduce), as Tertullian, Apollinaris and the greatest part of the Westerners maintain, so that just as body is born from body, so soul is born from soul and exists on a condition like that of the brute animals?
passages.notes: "dsiOQVOia" is a scanning garble of a Greek word, almost certainly ἀπόρροια ("emanation"), translated accordingly.

passages.original: super quo quid mihi uideretur, in opusculis contra Rufinum olim scripsisse me noui aduersus eum libellum, quem sanctae memoriae Anastasio, episcopo Romanae ecclesiae, dedit, in quo lubrica et subdola, immo stulta confessione, dum auditorum simplicitati inludere nititur, suae fidei, immo perfidiae, inlusit; quos libros reor sanctum parentem uestrum habere Oceanum. olim enim editi sunt multis Rufini libri aduersus nos calumnias respuentes. certe habes ibi uirum sanctum et eruditum Augustinum episcopum, qui uiua, ut aiunt, uoce doceie te poterit et suam, immo per se nostram, explicare sententiam.
passages.english: What I thought on this matter I know I once wrote in my short works against Rufinus, against the booklet which he gave to Anastasius of holy memory, bishop of the Roman church. In it, with a slippery and crafty, or rather foolish, confession, while he strives to make sport of the simplicity of his hearers, he made sport of his own faith, or rather faithlessness. I think your holy father Oceanus has these books, for they were published long ago, rebutting the slanders of Rufinus' many books against us. Certainly you have there the holy and learned man Bishop Augustine, who will be able to teach you with the living voice, as they say, and to explain his own view, or rather, through himself, ours.
passages.notes: "doceie" read as "docere".

passages.original: hoc autem anno, cum tres explicassem libros, subitus lmpetus barbarorum, de quibus tuus dicit Uergilius: lateque uagantes Barcaei et sancta scriptura de Ismahel: contra faciem omnium fratrum suorum habitabit, sic Aegypti limitem, Palaestinae, Phoenices, Syriae percucurrit ad instar torrentis cuncta secum trahens, ut uix manus eorum misericordia Christi potuerimus euadere.
passages.english: This year, however, when I had completed three books, a sudden onslaught of barbarians, of whom your Virgil says, "and the Barcaeans roaming far and wide," and holy Scripture says of Ishmael, "he will dwell over against the face of all his brothers," so overran the borders of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia and Syria, dragging everything with it like a torrent, that by the mercy of Christ we were barely able to escape their hands.
passages.notes: "lmpetus" read as "impetus".

passages.original: Catonem quoque — illum dico censorium et uestrae quondam urbis principem —, qui in extrema aetate Graecas litteras non erubuit censor nec desperauit senex discere *«*#*#**#•****#* et M. Crassum semel in uita scribit risisse Lucilius. fuerit illa affectata seueritas et gloriam quaerens auramque popularem; nos affectus et perturbationes, quamdiu in tabernaculo corporis huius habitamus et fragili carne circumdamur, moderari et regere possumus, amputare non possumus. unde et psalmista dicit: iras cimini nolite peccare, quod apostolus disserens: s o 1, inquit, non occidat super iracundiam uestram, quia et irasci hominis est et finem irae ponere Christiani.
passages.english: Cato too, I mean the Censor and once the leading man of your city, who in extreme old age was not ashamed, as censor, of Greek letters, nor despaired, as an old man, of learning [...]; and Lucilius writes that Marcus Crassus laughed once in his life. Let that have been an affected severity, seeking glory and popular favour; we, so long as we dwell in the tent of this body and are surrounded by fragile flesh, can moderate and govern our passions and disturbances, but cannot cut them off. Hence the psalmist too says: 'Be angry, and do not sin', which the apostle explaining says: 'Let not the sun go down upon your wrath', because both to be angry is human, and to put an end to anger is Christian.
passages.notes: A lacuna (row of asterisks) follows 'discere'; the sentence about Cato is incomplete. 'iras cimini' read as irascimini; 's o 1' as sol.

passages.original: ted, ut dicere coeperam, exponam breuiter principum et sociorum tuorum nomina, ut animaduertas, qualium consortium glorieris. Manicheus electos suos, quos inter aipidag Platonis in caelestibus conlocat, dicit omni carere peccato nec, si uelint, posse peccare; ad tanta enim eos uirtutum culmina transcendisse, ut carnis operibus inludant.
passages.english: But, as I had begun to say, I will briefly set out the names of your leaders and associates, so that you may notice in what kind of fellowship you glory. Manichaeus says that his Elect, whom he places in the heavens among the Ideas of Plato, lack all sin and cannot sin even if they wished; for they have risen to such heights of virtue that they mock the works of the flesh.
passages.notes: "ted" read as "sed". "aipidag" is a garbled Greek word; probably ἰδέας (Ideas), but the reading is uncertain.

passages.original: et iuxta illud Lucretii: ac ueluti pueris absinthia taetra medentes cum damus, prius ora circum inlinimus dulci mellis flauoque liquore, ita ille unum Iohannem in ipsius libri posuit principio, quem et catholicum et sanctum fuisse non dubium est, ut per illius occasionem ceteros, quos posuerat hereticos, ecclesiae introduceret.
passages.english: And, following that line of Lucretius, "and just as physicians, when we give bitter wormwood to children, first smear the rim of the cup around with the sweet and golden liquid of honey," so he placed John alone at the very beginning of his book, who without doubt was both catholic and holy, so that through him as a pretext he might bring into the Church the others he had listed, who were heretics.
passages.notes: The John and the author ("he") are not identified within the passage.
